chunks: Components of an embedded system. The question: What are some components/subsystems you'd find in an embedded system?
An embedded system is a small computer hidden inside a product, such as a thermostat or a washing machine.
Its job is to read inputs from the real world, decide what to do, and control outputs.
To do that, a processor needs memory to hold its program, power, a clock, a way to start cleanly, and connections to sensors and outputs.
Think of a small restaurant kitchen. The cook is the processor. The recipe book is the program memory, and the counter is the working space for the dish in progress.
Gas and electricity are the power, and the kitchen timer is the clock. Orders come in (inputs), and plates go out (outputs).
Every shift starts with the same opening routine, like a reset. Without any one of these, the cook can't work.
Power, clock, reset and debug all feed the MCU. Inputs, outputs and communication buses leave from it. When a board is dead, check the four arrows into the MCU first.
Embedded system: a computer built into a product to do one specific job.
Microcontroller (MCU): one chip holding the processor, memory and input/output hardware ("Microcontroller vs microprocessor").
Flash and RAM: flash keeps the program (the firmware) with the power off. RAM is working space that is wiped at power-off.
Clock: a steady tick that paces everything the chip does. Reset: a signal that puts the chip in a known starting state ("Reset signal: what and why").
A battery-powered temperature logger has a temperature sensor, a microcontroller that stores each reading, a coin cell for power, and a slow clock that wakes the chip every 10 seconds.
The chip is awake for 20 milliseconds (thousandths of a second) and draws 5 milliamps (thousandths of an amp). Over 10 seconds, that averages 10 microamps (millionths of an amp).
Sleep adds about 1. 5 microamps. A coin cell rated 220 milliamp hours can supply 1 milliamps for 220 hours, so this lasts about two years, an upper estimate.
That is the whole idea.
"An embedded system is a processor, usually an MCU, with its memory, plus the supporting blocks that make it run: power and decoupling, a clock, reset, and a debug port.
Around that are inputs, like sensors and buttons, and outputs like LEDs, motors and displays, plus communication buses such as I2C, SPI, UART, CAN and USB.
Protection like ESD, a watchdog and brown-out detection makes it robust, and the firmware, including drivers, a bootloader and maybe an RTOS, is the last component."
